# SK3031 — The method is `async` only to return an awaited task

<!-- Generated from Rules/Rikarin.Skala.Rules.Metadata/rules.json. Do not edit. -->

The method's whole body is `return await X()`, so the `async` state machine exists only to hand back a task the method already had.

| | |
|---|---|
| Category | Async |
| Default severity | suggestion |
| Scope | Semantic |
| Needs a compilation | yes |
| Fix | yes, review it |
| Language version floor | — |
| Since | 1.3 |

## Why

An `async` method compiles to a state machine, an allocation and a resumption path. Where the entire body is one `await` whose result is returned unchanged, all of that exists to give the caller a task the method was holding already. Returning it directly removes the machinery and does the same work.

## Example

Instead of:

```csharp
async Task<int> ReadAsync(Stream source) {
    return await source.ReadAsync(buffer);
}
```

Write:

```csharp
Task<int> ReadAsync(Stream source) {
    return source.ReadAsync(buffer);
}
```

## When it does not fire

⚠ **The fix is unsafe and the reason is not the edit.** Eliding the `await` moves exceptions from the returned task to the call — a method that used to fault its task now throws synchronously, at a place the caller may not be catching — and drops the method from every stack trace the task carries. Both are behaviour, both are usually acceptable, and neither is a decision a tool makes. ⚠ **It is outright wrong inside a `using`, which is what `SK3007` reports, and the two are disjoint by construction.** The body matched here must be a *single* statement that is the `return await`, or a single expression body: a `using` declaration needs a statement before the return, and a `using` statement makes the block's one statement a `using` rather than a `return`, so no shape this rule reports can contain one. `supersedes` would be the wrong instrument regardless — `Supersession.Apply` suppresses the *superseded* finding, which is the one carrying the remedy. ⚠ **The operand's type must be the declared return type, not merely awaitable to it.** `await GetValueTask()` inside an `async Task<int>` is legal and `return GetValueTask()` is not; the same test is what excludes `.ConfigureAwait(false)`, whose type is a configured awaitable rather than a task. ⚠ **A nested `await` in the operand withdraws it**: `return await Read(await Open());` would leave an `await` in a method that is no longer `async`, which is CS4032 — a fix that parses and does not compile. ⚠ Only ordinary methods and local functions; `partial`, `abstract` and `extern` are skipped, and lambdas are not matched at all. ⚠ A comment between `async` and the return type, or between `await` and its operand, withdraws the finding rather than being deleted with the keyword.
